To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the interaction of the antimicrobial peptides with dipal mitoylphosph atidylglycer o l–polyd iacet ylen e vesicles is an effective tool for screening antimicrobial peptides, and that fatty acid conjugation and amino acid substitution in the antimicrobial peptides have a direct effect on their interaction with phospholipid vesicles and, consequently, on their antimicrobial activity against different strains of Staph. aureus and L. monocytogenes.
the interaction of antimicrobial peptides with phospholipid vesicles can be used to predict their activity against bacterial strains.

the conjugation of the peptides with short fatty acids improved the antimicrobial activity against S. aureus and L. monocytogenes strains, and the interaction of these lipopeptides with phospholipid bilayers was higher than the interaction of the parent peptides.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a bioassay that is capable to evaluate the interaction between antimicrobial peptides and phospholipids, which can be used to design new peptides with specific activity against different bacterial strains.
the design of antimicrobial peptide analogs with improved antimicrobial activity against Gram‐positive bacterial strains and with a better interaction with biomimetic membranes.
the design and synthesis of new antimicrobial peptides and their evaluation as antimicrobial agents.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the interaction of the lipopeptides with the polydiacetylene membrane is a suitable tool for evaluating differences in the interaction with biological and biomimetical membranes and for the prediction of the antimicrobial activity of the peptides against Staphyloccoccus aureus strain, but not for the prediction of their activity against Listeria monocitogenes strain.
the bioassay is a useful tool for the evaluation of the antimicrobial activity and membrane interaction of antimicrobial peptides.
the polydiacetylene bioassay can be a valuable tool for screening antimicrobial peptides, but it should be used as a complementary method to other techniques.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the interaction of the peptide analogs with the polydiacetylene system can provide information on the interaction of the antimicrobial peptide with the bacterial membrane, and this interaction correlates with the biological properties of these peptides.
the polydiacetylene assay is useful to detect the effect of amino acid substitution and acylation of antimicrobial peptides with short fatty acids in the interaction with biological membranes.
fatty acid conjugation of antimicrobial peptides is a promising strategy to improve their activity and selectivity.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the bioassay is a useful tool to detect differences in interaction of the peptides, associated with the amino acid substitution and the N‐terminal conjugations with different fatty acids, with dipalmitolylphosphatidglycerol– and dipalmitolylephatidylcholin–polydiacelylene vesicles.
the interaction of antimicrobial peptides with polydiacetylene liposomes provides a simple and fast method to detect differences in their interaction with phospholipid vesicles.
polydiacetylene‐based bioassays can be successfully used to detect differences in peptide interaction with phospholipid membranes, which can be correlated with their antimicrobial activity.
